title: Lemma 20.8.11
text: Lemma 20.8.11 . 90BA432FB977 Let $\mu :Z\to X$ be a composition of smooth-center blowups, and let $\widetilde D$ be the strict transform of a prime divisor $D$. Assume that $\mu $ is an isomorphism near a general point of $D$. Then \[  \langle (\mu ^*\alpha )^{n-1}\rangle _{Z\mid \widetilde D} =\langle \alpha ^{n-1}\rangle _{X\mid D}.  \] Proof. The generic minimal Lelong number along the two divisors is the same. One inequality follows by pullback. For the other, push forward a positive current in $\mu ^*\alpha $ and use the isomorphism near the generic point. For a big class the generic minimal Lelong number is the infimum over its positive currents. Thus either both divisors lie in the respective non-nef loci, in which case both sides are zero by definition, or neither does. Work in the latter case. Fix Kähler forms $\omega $ on $X$ and $\eta $ on $Z$. There is $C>0$ with $\mu ^*\omega \leq C\eta $. If $T\in \alpha $ has analytic singularities, $T\geq -\varepsilon \omega $, and no pole containing $D$, then \[  \mu ^*T+C\varepsilon \eta \geq \mu ^*(T+\varepsilon \omega )\geq 0.  \] Off the exceptional set, pullback preserves the restricted integral; that set has zero measure on the strict transform. Taking the suprema and then $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ gives the inequality from left to right with $\geq $. For the reverse inequality we can choose \[  [\eta ]=\mu ^*(\lambda [\omega ])-\{ F\} ,\qquad F\geq 0 \text{ exceptional},  \] with $\eta $ Kähler, by successive blowup metrics and a sufficiently large $\lambda $. Let $S\in \mu ^*\alpha $ be a numerical competitor with $S\geq -\varepsilon \eta $ and no pole containing $\widetilde D$, and set $R=S+\varepsilon \eta $. The positive current $U=\mu _*R$ has class $\alpha +\varepsilon \lambda [\omega ]$. Moreover EB71078BBAFF 20.8.12 \begin{equation}  \mu ^*U=R+\varepsilon [F]. \end{equation} Indeed $R+\varepsilon [F]$ is positive in the pullback class $\mu ^*(\alpha +\varepsilon \lambda [\omega ])$. By the correspondence of potentials under a modification of a smooth target , it equals the pullback of its pushforward. That pushforward is $U$, since an exceptional divisor pushes forward to zero. This proves the formula. Gently regularize $U$ by less singular analytic currents $U_ j$ with positivity loss $\delta _ j\omega \to 0$. Its generic Lelong number along $D$ is zero, so the approximants have no pole containing $D$. After adding $2\delta _ j\omega $, pullback and the restricted monotonicity theorem, applied to ( 20.8.12 ), give \[  \operatorname {Vol}_{X\mid D} (\alpha +(\varepsilon \lambda +2\delta _ j)[\omega ]) \geq \int _{\widetilde D} \left\langle (R|_{\widetilde D})^{n-1}\right\rangle .  \] Here one may first keep the extra $\delta _ j\mu ^*\omega $ on the right; positivity only enlarges that mass. The equality of the base restricted integral with its pullback is computed on the regular isomorphism locus. All omitted sets are analytic and receive no non-pluripolar mass. Classical restricted volume on the left is well defined: $U_ j+2\delta _ j\omega \geq \delta _ j\omega $ is a Kähler current smooth at a general point of $D$. Let $j\to \infty $ and then $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, or choose a diagonal $\delta _ j=o(\varepsilon )$. Monotonicity of the defining one-sided numerical suprema makes the left side converge to $\langle \alpha ^{n-1}\rangle _{X\mid D}$; the right-side suprema converge to the numerical restricted volume upstairs. This proves the opposite inequality and the lemma. $\square$

title: Equation 20.8.12

title: Lemma 20.8.13
text: Lemma 20.8.13 . DA69AEE4E88A Let $\mu :Y\to X$ be a modification and let $F$ be an effective $\mu $-exceptional real divisor. For a big class $\alpha $, \[  \operatorname {Vol}(\mu ^*\alpha +t\{ F\} )=\operatorname {Vol}(\alpha ) \quad (t\geq 0), \qquad \langle (\mu ^*\alpha )^{n-1}\rangle \cdot \{ F\} =0.  \] Proof. Pulling back a positive current in $\alpha $ and adding $t[F]$ proves the inequality $\geq $: the absolutely continuous top mass is unchanged over the common isomorphism locus. Conversely, pushing forward any positive current in $\mu ^*\alpha +t\{ F\} $ gives a positive current in $\alpha $, with the same absolutely continuous top mass on that locus. The exceptional analytic sets have Lebesgue measure zero, so the reverse inequality follows from the defining supremum of volume. This also proves birational invariance of volume when $t=0$. The derivative formula in theorem 10.99.8 on the big cone, applied on $Y$, identifies the right derivative at $t=0$ with $n\langle (\mu ^*\alpha )^{n-1}\rangle \cdot \{ F\} $. The displayed constant-volume identity makes that derivative zero. $\square$

title: Lemma 20.8.14
text: Lemma 20.8.14 . B50F0B700160 For a big class $\beta $ and its divisorial negative part $N(\beta )$, \[  \langle \beta ^{n-1}\rangle \cdot \{ N(\beta )\} =0.  \] Proof. Let $T_{\min }\in \beta $ have minimal singularities. Its generic divisor coefficients are those of $N(\beta )$, so Siu decomposition gives $T_{\min }-s[N(\beta )]\geq 0$ for $0\leq s\leq 1$. Only finitely many divisors occur: their support is contained in that of any gently analytic Kähler current in the big class. Removing their integration currents does not change the non-pluripolar top mass, because the currents agree off those divisors and all the products give the divisors zero mass. The maximal-mass characterization of volume thus gives \[  \operatorname {Vol}(\beta -s\{ N(\beta )\} ) \geq \int _ X\langle (T_{\min }-s[N(\beta )])^ n\rangle =\operatorname {Vol}(\beta ).  \] The reverse inequality is pseudoeffective monotonicity of volume. These classes are big since their volume is positive. Differentiate the constant-volume identity at $s=0$ using theorem 10.99.8 . The derivative is $-n\langle \beta ^{n-1}\rangle \cdot \{ N(\beta )\} $, proving the claim. $\square$

title: Lemma 20.8.15
text: Lemma 20.8.15 . 41D346BEA9CE For a big class $\alpha $ and a prime divisor $D\subset E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha )$, \[  \langle \alpha ^{n-1}\rangle \cdot \{ D\} =0.  \] Proof. For every sufficiently small $\varepsilon >0$, the class $\beta _\varepsilon =\alpha -\varepsilon [\omega ]$ is big. Its minimal generic Lelong number along $D$ is strictly positive. Indeed, if it were zero, Demailly's gentle analytic regularization of a current with minimal singularities in $\beta _\varepsilon $ would give a current $T_ j\in \beta _\varepsilon $ with $T_ j\geq -\frac12\varepsilon \omega $, analytic singularities, and zero generic Lelong number along $D$. A gentle approximant is smooth off its analytic pole set, and zero generic Lelong number means that this pole set does not contain $D$. Hence it is smooth near a general point of $D$, and $T_ j+\varepsilon \omega $ would be a Kähler current in $\alpha $ smooth at such a point, contrary to $D\subset E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha )$. Thus $D$ occurs with a positive coefficient in $N(\beta _\varepsilon )$. The preceding lemma 20.8.14 gives \[  \langle \beta _\varepsilon ^{n-1}\rangle \cdot N(\beta _\varepsilon )=0.  \] Each summand in this pairing is nonnegative: the positive-product class is a limit of pushforwards of nef powers, and its pairing with any effective divisor is nonnegative. The positive coefficient of $D$ therefore forces $\langle \beta _\varepsilon ^{n-1}\rangle \cdot \{ D\} =0$. The continuous full volume-gradient formula now allows $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, proving the assertion. $\square$

title: Proposition 20.8.16
search_title: Restricted equality from smooth divisor derivative
text: Proposition 20.8.16 . 7ED04B77FCC6 Let $\alpha $ be big on a compact Kähler manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$. For every prime divisor $D$, \[  \langle \alpha ^{n-1}\rangle _{X\mid D} =\langle \alpha ^{n-1}\rangle \cdot \{ D\} , \qquad \langle \alpha ^{n-1}\rangle _{X\mid D}=0 \  \Longleftrightarrow \  D\subset E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha ).  \] Proof. For $n=1$, work on the connected component containing the point $D$. The top real cohomology is one dimensional, and a big class has positive degree, so it is a positive multiple of a Kähler class. Its non-Kähler locus is empty, its positive product of order zero is $1$, and the zero-dimensional restricted mass of $D$ is $1$. Both assertions follow. Hence assume $n\geq 2$. First suppose $D\not\subset E_{\mathrm{nn}}(\alpha )$. For each $\varepsilon >0$, regularization of a minimal current in $\alpha $ with zero generic Lelong number along $D$, followed by addition of $\varepsilon \omega $, gives a Kähler current in $\alpha _\varepsilon =\alpha +\varepsilon [\omega ]$ smooth near a general point of $D$. Thus $D$ meets its Kähler locus. Resolve $D$ by a modification $\mu :Z\to X$ which is an isomorphism near a general point of $D$, and write $\mu ^*D=\widetilde D+F$, with $F\geq 0$ exceptional and $\widetilde D$ smooth. The strict transform meets the Kähler locus of $\mu ^*\alpha _\varepsilon $. For completeness, a Kähler current smooth generically on $D$ pulls back to a current dominating $\delta \mu ^*\omega $; the standard exceptional logarithmic correction on the resolution replaces this by a Kähler lower bound, adding only exceptional poles. No pole contains $\widetilde D$. Apply theorem 20.8.3 on $Z$ and the full volume-gradient formula theorem 10.99.8 there. Birational invariance of restricted volume lemma 20.8.11 , then lemma 20.8.13 , give \[  \langle \alpha _\varepsilon ^{n-1}\rangle _{X\mid D} =\langle (\mu ^*\alpha _\varepsilon )^{n-1}\rangle \cdot \{ \widetilde D\}  =\langle (\mu ^*\alpha _\varepsilon )^{n-1}\rangle \cdot \mu ^*\{ D\} .  \] Birational invariance of volume for all small perturbations in the direction $\{ D\} $ and its differentiability identify the last expression with $\langle \alpha _\varepsilon ^{n-1}\rangle \cdot \{ D\} $. The defining one-sided limit for numerical restricted volume gives \[  \lim _{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \langle \alpha _\varepsilon ^{n-1}\rangle _{X\mid D} =\langle \alpha ^{n-1}\rangle _{X\mid D}.  \] Indeed, if $F(s)$ is the defining supremum over positive currents with analytic singularities in $\alpha +s[\omega ]$ whose poles do not contain $D$, then $F$ is increasing and the two sides are respectively $\lim _{\varepsilon \downarrow 0}\lim _{s\downarrow \varepsilon }F(s)$ and $\lim _{s\downarrow 0}F(s)$. They agree by monotonicity. Continuity of the full volume gradient proves the desired equality. If $D\subset E_{\mathrm{nn}}(\alpha )$, the numerical restricted volume is zero by definition. The coefficient of $D$ in $N(\alpha )$ is positive, so lemma 20.8.14 and the nonnegativity of the separate divisor pairings give $\langle \alpha ^{n-1}\rangle \cdot \{ D\} =0$ as well. It remains to identify the zero locus. Containment in the non-Kähler locus gives zero positive-product pairing by lemma 20.8.15 , and therefore zero restricted volume by the equality already proved. Otherwise a Kähler current $T\in \alpha $, with the permitted analytic singularities and no pole containing $D$, satisfies $T\geq \delta \omega $ for some $\delta >0$. It is an admissible competitor, and its restricted integral is at least $\delta ^{n-1}\int _ D\omega ^{n-1}>0$. This proves the converse. $\square$

title: 10.101 Balanced forms and movable classes
text: Let $X$ be a connected compact Kähler manifold of dimension $n\geq 2$. Write $H^{p,p}_{\mathbb R}(X)$ for real Bott–Chern cohomology, identified with the real $(p,p)$ part of de Rham cohomology. The Kähler $\partial \bar\partial $ lemma, in the form of Bott–Chern, Dolbeault and Aeppli cohomology on a compact Kähler manifold , also identifies \[  H^{1,1}_{\mathbb R}(X) \simeq H_ A^{1,1}(X,\mathbb R) =\frac{\{ T\text{ real of type }(1,1):\partial \bar\partial T=0\} }{\{ \partial \overline S+\bar\partial S:S\text{ of type }(1,0)\} }.  \] The same quotients may be formed with smooth forms or currents. These are the Kähler cohomology identifications. Let $\mathcal P_ A$ be the cone of Aeppli classes of positive $\partial \bar\partial $-closed $(1,1)$-currents, and let $\mathcal B$ be the set of classes of smooth strictly positive closed $(n-1,n-1)$-forms. The positive-matrix root formula in the proof of the Gauduchon criterion for positivity identifies these forms exactly with $\gamma ^{n-1}$ for balanced Hermitian metrics $\gamma $. Here and below all pairings are integration, with the same fixed normalization of $dd^ c$ on the two factors. Lemma 10.101.1 . 255F6B93CCE9 The cone $\mathcal P_ A$ is closed and contains no line. Under the integration pairing, \[  \mathcal B=\operatorname {Int}(\mathcal P_ A^\vee ), \qquad \overline{\mathcal B}=\mathcal P_ A^\vee .  \] Proof. Fix a Kähler form $\omega $. If $T\geq 0$, then $\int _ XT\wedge \omega ^{n-1}$ is its trace mass, is zero only for $T=0$, and depends only on the Aeppli class of $T$. Consequently, positive currents in a bounded set of Aeppli classes have bounded trace masses. Weak compactness for positive currents and continuity of pairing with smooth closed forms show that $\mathcal P_ A$ is closed. The positive mass functional also proves that it contains no line and that a positive current of zero Aeppli class is zero. If $\Gamma $ is smooth strictly positive and closed, then $\Gamma \geq \varepsilon \omega ^{n-1}$ for some $\varepsilon >0$. Thus $\int _ X\Gamma \wedge T>0$ for every nonzero positive $\partial \bar\partial $-closed current $T$. Conversely, suppose that $b\in H^{n-1,n-1}_{\mathbb R}(X)$ pairs strictly positively with every nonzero element of $\mathcal P_ A$. Choose a smooth real closed representative $\rho $ of $b$. If no representative of $b$ were strictly positive, the affine space \[  \rho +dd^ c C^\infty _{n-2,n-2}(X,\mathbb R)  \] would be disjoint from the open convex cone of smooth strictly positive $(n-1,n-1)$-forms. The $\partial \bar\partial $ lemma says that this affine space consists of all smooth representatives of $b$ of the given type. Hahn–Banach separation, with its sign chosen positive on the open cone, gives a nonzero continuous real linear functional $T$ such that \[  T(dd^ c\Psi )=0\quad \hbox{for every smooth real }\Psi , \qquad T(\rho )\leq 0, \qquad T(\Gamma )\geq 0\quad (\Gamma >0).  \] Indeed, the affine directions force the first equality; scaling the positive cone and then taking its closure gives the other two inequalities. This functional is a positive $(1,1)$-current and $dd^ cT=0$. Its Aeppli class is nonzero by the mass observation, contrary to the strict positivity assumption on $b$. Therefore $b\in \mathcal B$. The trace-one slice of $\mathcal P_ A$ is compact: it is the image of the weakly compact set of positive pluriharmonic currents of mass one. Strict positivity on this slice is consequently equivalent to membership in the interior of the dual cone. Finally $[\omega ^{n-1}]$ belongs to this interior, so every element $b$ of $\mathcal P_ A^\vee $ is a limit of $b+\varepsilon [\omega ^{n-1}]\in \mathcal B$. This proves both assertions. $\square$ Proposition 10.101.2 . 8DC16DCAD850 The balanced and movable cones satisfy \[  \overline{\mathcal B}=\mathcal M, \qquad \mathcal B=\operatorname {Int}\mathcal M.  \] Moreover, $\mathcal M$ is the closed convex cone generated by the classes $\mu _*(\kappa ^{n-1})$, where $\mu :Y\to X$ is a modification from a compact Kähler manifold and $\kappa $ is a Kähler class on $Y$. Proof. Let $j:H^{1,1}_{\mathbb R}(X)\to H_ A^{1,1}(X,\mathbb R)$ be the cohomology identification. A closed positive current is pluriharmonic, so $j(\mathcal E)\subseteq \mathcal P_ A$. For the reverse inclusion, let $T\geq 0$ be pluriharmonic and let $a=j^{-1}[T]_ A$. For a modification $\mu :Y\to X$ and Kähler forms $\omega _1,\ldots ,\omega _{n-1}$ on $Y$, choose a positive pluriharmonic current $\widetilde T$ in $\mu ^*[T]_ A$ by theorem 5.66.2 . Smooth closed test forms annihilate Aeppli boundaries, hence \[  a\cdot \mu _*[\omega _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \omega _{n-1}] =\int _ Y\widetilde T\wedge \omega _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \omega _{n-1} \geq 0.  \] Cone duality theorem 10.100.1 gives $a\in \mathcal E$. Thus $j(\mathcal E)=\mathcal P_ A$. Apply lemma 10.101.1 and $\mathcal E^\vee =\mathcal M$ to conclude. The single-power description is also theorem 10.100.1 . $\square$

title: 6.49 Polynomial iterates and residual mass
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
text:
Use $dd^ c=\mathrm i\partial  ar\partial /(2\pi )$ and the classical Monge–Ampère product, including mass at an isolated pole. For $\zeta \in \mathbb C^2$ put $L(\zeta )=\log \max \{ |\zeta _1|^2,|\zeta _2|^2\} $, with $L(0)=-\infty $. By the anisotropic logarithmic-pole formula , $(dd^ cL)^2=\delta _0$. Proposition 6.49.1 . CE621FA6CE58 For every $\varepsilon \in \mathbb C$ the polynomial map \[  F_\varepsilon (z,w)=\left( rac{w^2}{2},  rac{z^2}{2}+\varepsilon wight)  \] is proper, surjective, and has at most four points in each fiber. Its degree is four and $F_\varepsilon ^{-1}(0)=\{ 0\} $. At a fiber point $(z,w)$ its local degree is \[  e(F_\varepsilon ,(z,w))= (1+\mathbf1_{\{ w=0\} })(1+\mathbf1_{\{ z=0\} }).  \] In particular its local degree at the origin is four. Proof. For a target $(\alpha , eta )$ the equations are \[  w^2=2\alpha ,\qquad z^2=2 eta -2\varepsilon w.  \] First choose a square root $w$, and then a square root $z$. This proves surjectivity and the fiber bound, including repeated roots. Moreover \[  |w|\leq (2|\alpha |)^{1/2},\qquad |z|\leq  igl (2| eta |+2|\varepsilon |(2|\alpha |)^{1/2} igr )^{1/2}.  \] The inverse image of a compact set is therefore closed and bounded, hence compact. This proves properness. The zero fiber is visibly the origin. The complex Jacobian determinant is $-zw$. If $\varepsilon 
e 0$, exclude the target set \[  B_\varepsilon =\{ \alpha =0\} \cup \{  eta ^2=2\varepsilon ^2\alpha \} ;  \] if $\varepsilon =0$, exclude $\{ \alpha  eta =0\} $. These are proper closed null sets. Outside them both square-root choices at each step are distinct and nonzero, so there are exactly four regular preimages. The inverse function theorem supplies the four sheets. For the local assertion, choose small disjoint discs about the possible values of $w$ and $z$ in the fixed fiber. Near a nonzero root the square equation has one local branch; near its zero root it has two roots for every sufficiently small generic nonzero right-hand side. First count the $w$ roots in its chosen disc, then the $z$ roots in its disc. Their right-hand sides tend to the fixed values uniformly in the finitely many first choices. Thus all these roots lie in the chosen product neighborhood for sufficiently small target perturbations. The number of regular points there is the displayed product. This is the local topological degree; the same argument shows that the local degrees in every fiber sum to four. No multiplicity of an algebraic quotient is assumed. $\square$ Corollary 6.49.2 . A9F7692E230F Let $\varepsilon _1,\ldots ,\varepsilon _ j\in \mathbb C$ and put $H_ j=F_{\varepsilon _ j}\circ \cdots \circ F_{\varepsilon _1}$. Then $H_ j$ is proper and surjective, its fibers are finite, its degree and local degree at zero are $4^ j$, and its zero fiber is $\{ 0\} $. Its classical logarithmic measure is \[   igl (dd^ c\log \| H_ j\| _\infty ^2 igr )^2=4^ j\delta _0.  \] Proof. Compositions of proper maps are proper: inverse images of compact sets are obtained by successive compact inverse images. The same reasoning gives surjectivity, finite fibers and the asserted zero fiber. The sheet count also follows directly. Put $B_1=B_{\varepsilon _1}$ and inductively \[  B_ j=B_{\varepsilon _ j}\cup F_{\varepsilon _ j}(B_{j-1}).  \] These sets are closed, by properness, and null. Indeed, a polynomial map is Lipschitz on each compact box in $\mathbb R^4$, and cube covers of a null set show that a Lipschitz map in the same real dimension has null image. A countable box cover proves the claim. Every target outside $B_ j$ has four regular preimages under the last map, all outside $B_{j-1}$. Induction gives $4^ j$ distinct regular preimages under $H_ j$. Its Jacobian is nonzero there, and its degree is $4^ j$. For local degrees, choose disjoint neighborhoods of the finitely many intermediate fiber points. Properness excludes other points over a sufficiently small target neighborhood. Counting the nearby regular preimages at each step multiplies the local degrees just proved. In particular the unique zero fiber has local degree $4\cdots 4=4^ j$. Equivalently, for every neighborhood $V$ of zero, all preimages of sufficiently small target points lie in $V$: otherwise properness would give a nonzero limit point in the zero fiber. Thus all $4^ j$ nearby sheets belong to the local degree there. Apply the proper sheet-degree formula the proper hypersurface degree formula to the prime hypersurface $D=\mathbb C^2	imes \{ 0\} $ in $\mathbb C^2	imes \mathbb C$ and the map $(\zeta ,t)\mapsto H_ j(\zeta )$. Its restriction to $D$ is proper, and the sheet count just proved gives $(H_ j)_*1=4^ j1$. For $T>0$ set $L_ T=\max \{ L,-2T\} $. The bounded continuous projection identity in the weighted projection formula therefore gives \[  (H_ j)_* igl (dd^ c(L_ T\circ H_ j) igr )^2 =4^ j(dd^ cL_ T)^2.  \] Both decreasing limits have only the isolated pole zero. The classical decreasing continuity of the theorem on classical products with compact unbounded loci applies: coordinate balls around the pole have boundaries on which these weights are bounded, and smaller balls suffice elsewhere. If $\chi \in C_ c(\mathbb C^2)$, properness makes $\chi \circ H_ j$ compactly supported as well. Consequently weak convergence can be passed through this particular pushforward, giving \[  (H_ j)_* igl (dd^ c(L\circ H_ j) igr )^2=4^ j\delta _0.  \] No mass can be lost at infinity in this step. Positivity forces the upstairs measure to be supported on $H_ j^{-1}(0)=\{ 0\} $: for a compact set disjoint from zero choose a target cutoff supported away from zero and equal to one on its image. A target cutoff equal to one near zero identifies its atom as $4^ j$. This proves the claimed identity on all of $\mathbb C^2$. $\square$ Definition 6.49.3 . 54F98147B130 For $j\geq 1$ set \[  \varepsilon _ j= rac14\exp (-8^{j-1}),\qquad c_ j=\prod _{k=1}^ j\varepsilon _ k =4^{-j}\exp \! \left(- rac{8^ j-1}{7}ight),  \] and define on $\mathbb C^2$ \[  H_ j=F_{\varepsilon _ j}\circ \cdots \circ F_{\varepsilon _1},\qquad p_ j=2^{-j}\log \| H_ j\| _\infty ^2,\qquad p_ j(0)=-\infty .  \] Write $e_2=(0,1)$. Proposition 6.49.4 . DDF1EA12A4BF Each $p_ j$ is negative psh on the unit bidisc, continuous off zero, and tends to $-\infty $ at zero. In the normalization $
u (v,0)=\liminf _{\zeta 	o 0}v(\zeta )/\log \| \zeta \| ^2$, it satisfies \[  
u (p_ j,0)=2^{-j},\qquad (dd^ cp_ j)^2=\delta _0.  \] Every finite sublevel of $p_ j$ is relatively compact in $\mathbb C^2$. Moreover \[  dH_ j(0)e_2=c_ je_2,\qquad \| H_ j(te_2)\| _\infty \geq c_ jt\quad (0<t<1).  \] Proof. The preceding corollary and homogeneity give $(dd^ cp_ j)^2=2^{-2j}4^ j\delta _0=\delta _0$ on $\mathbb C^2$. For $r=\| (z,w)\| _\infty \leq 1$ and $0<\varepsilon \leq 1/4$, \[  \| F_\varepsilon (z,w)\| _\infty \leq 	frac 12r^2+	frac 14r\leq 	frac 34.  \] Thus each map takes the unit bidisc into itself. The maximum of the two holomorphic component logarithms is plurisubharmonic. The zero-fiber statement gives the continuity and pole assertions. Closed finite sublevels of $p_ j$ are inverse images under the globally proper $H_ j$ of compact closed bidiscs, so they are compact. At zero $dF_\varepsilon =\operatorname {diag}(0,\varepsilon )$, so the chain rule proves the derivative formula. Along $(0,t)$ write $H_ k(0,t)=(z_ k,w_ k)$, with $(z_0,w_0)=(0,t)$. The recursion \[  z_ k=w_{k-1}^2/2,\qquad w_ k=z_{k-1}^2/2+\varepsilon _ kw_{k-1}  \] keeps both coordinates nonnegative and gives $w_ k\geq \varepsilon _ kw_{k-1}$, proving the last bound. Since $H_ j$ is holomorphic and vanishes at zero, a derivative bound on a small ball gives $\| H_ j(\zeta )\| _\infty \leq C_ j\| \zeta \| $. Dividing the resulting upper bound for $p_ j$ by the negative $\log \| \zeta \| ^2$ gives a lower limit at least $2^{-j}$. On the line $\zeta =te_2$, the derivative formula gives $H_ j(te_2)=c_ jte_2+O(t^2)$, so that the ratio tends to $2^{-j}$ there. The logarithmic characterization of the Lelong number, Lelong numbers as logarithmic growth slopes , proves the equality. Changing between the Euclidean and maximum norm adds a bounded term to the denominator and does not change this limit. $\square$ All pushforwards above use globally proper maps on $\mathbb C^2$. The unit-bidisc conclusions follow by locality after that calculation; no properness of the bidisc-to-bidisc restriction is assumed.

title: Proposition 6.49.1
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
text: Proposition 6.49.1 . CE621FA6CE58 For every $\varepsilon \in \mathbb C$ the polynomial map \[  F_\varepsilon (z,w)=\left(\frac{w^2}{2}, \frac{z^2}{2}+\varepsilon w\right)  \] is proper, surjective, and has at most four points in each fiber. Its degree is four and $F_\varepsilon ^{-1}(0)=\{ 0\} $. At a fiber point $(z,w)$ its local degree is \[  e(F_\varepsilon ,(z,w))= (1+\mathbf1_{\{ w=0\} })(1+\mathbf1_{\{ z=0\} }).  \] In particular its local degree at the origin is four. Proof. For a target $(\alpha ,\beta )$ the equations are \[  w^2=2\alpha ,\qquad z^2=2\beta -2\varepsilon w.  \] First choose a square root $w$, and then a square root $z$. This proves surjectivity and the fiber bound, including repeated roots. Moreover \[  |w|\leq (2|\alpha |)^{1/2},\qquad |z|\leq \bigl (2|\beta |+2|\varepsilon |(2|\alpha |)^{1/2}\bigr )^{1/2}.  \] The inverse image of a compact set is therefore closed and bounded, hence compact. This proves properness. The zero fiber is visibly the origin. The complex Jacobian determinant is $-zw$. If $\varepsilon \ne 0$, exclude the target set \[  B_\varepsilon =\{ \alpha =0\} \cup \{ \beta ^2=2\varepsilon ^2\alpha \} ;  \] if $\varepsilon =0$, exclude $\{ \alpha \beta =0\} $. These are proper closed null sets. Outside them both square-root choices at each step are distinct and nonzero, so there are exactly four regular preimages. The inverse function theorem supplies the four sheets. For the local assertion, choose small disjoint discs about the possible values of $w$ and $z$ in the fixed fiber. Near a nonzero root the square equation has one local branch; near its zero root it has two roots for every sufficiently small generic nonzero right-hand side. First count the $w$ roots in its chosen disc, then the $z$ roots in its disc. Their right-hand sides tend to the fixed values uniformly in the finitely many first choices. Thus all these roots lie in the chosen product neighborhood for sufficiently small target perturbations. The number of regular points there is the displayed product. This is the local topological degree; the same argument shows that the local degrees in every fiber sum to four. No multiplicity of an algebraic quotient is assumed. $\square$

title: Corollary 6.49.2
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
text: Corollary 6.49.2 . A9F7692E230F Let $\varepsilon _1,\ldots ,\varepsilon _ j\in \mathbb C$ and put $H_ j=F_{\varepsilon _ j}\circ \cdots \circ F_{\varepsilon _1}$. Then $H_ j$ is proper and surjective, its fibers are finite, its degree and local degree at zero are $4^ j$, and its zero fiber is $\{ 0\} $. Its classical logarithmic measure is \[  \bigl (dd^ c\log \| H_ j\| _\infty ^2\bigr )^2=4^ j\delta _0.  \] Proof. Compositions of proper maps are proper: inverse images of compact sets are obtained by successive compact inverse images. The same reasoning gives surjectivity, finite fibers and the asserted zero fiber. The sheet count also follows directly. Put $B_1=B_{\varepsilon _1}$ and inductively \[  B_ j=B_{\varepsilon _ j}\cup F_{\varepsilon _ j}(B_{j-1}).  \] These sets are closed, by properness, and null. Indeed, a polynomial map is Lipschitz on each compact box in $\mathbb R^4$, and cube covers of a null set show that a Lipschitz map in the same real dimension has null image. A countable box cover proves the claim. Every target outside $B_ j$ has four regular preimages under the last map, all outside $B_{j-1}$. Induction gives $4^ j$ distinct regular preimages under $H_ j$. Its Jacobian is nonzero there, and its degree is $4^ j$. For local degrees, choose disjoint neighborhoods of the finitely many intermediate fiber points. Properness excludes other points over a sufficiently small target neighborhood. Counting the nearby regular preimages at each step multiplies the local degrees just proved. In particular the unique zero fiber has local degree $4\cdots 4=4^ j$. Equivalently, for every neighborhood $V$ of zero, all preimages of sufficiently small target points lie in $V$: otherwise properness would give a nonzero limit point in the zero fiber. Thus all $4^ j$ nearby sheets belong to the local degree there. Apply the proper sheet-degree formula the proper hypersurface degree formula to the prime hypersurface $D=\mathbb C^2\times \{ 0\} $ in $\mathbb C^2\times \mathbb C$ and the map $(\zeta ,t)\mapsto H_ j(\zeta )$. Its restriction to $D$ is proper, and the sheet count just proved gives $(H_ j)_*1=4^ j1$. For $T>0$ set $L_ T=\max \{ L,-2T\} $. The bounded continuous projection identity in the weighted projection formula therefore gives \[  (H_ j)_*\bigl (dd^ c(L_ T\circ H_ j)\bigr )^2 =4^ j(dd^ cL_ T)^2.  \] Both decreasing limits have only the isolated pole zero. The classical decreasing continuity of the theorem on classical products with compact unbounded loci applies: coordinate balls around the pole have boundaries on which these weights are bounded, and smaller balls suffice elsewhere. If $\chi \in C_ c(\mathbb C^2)$, properness makes $\chi \circ H_ j$ compactly supported as well. Consequently weak convergence can be passed through this particular pushforward, giving \[  (H_ j)_*\bigl (dd^ c(L\circ H_ j)\bigr )^2=4^ j\delta _0.  \] No mass can be lost at infinity in this step. Positivity forces the upstairs measure to be supported on $H_ j^{-1}(0)=\{ 0\} $: for a compact set disjoint from zero choose a target cutoff supported away from zero and equal to one on its image. A target cutoff equal to one near zero identifies its atom as $4^ j$. This proves the claimed identity on all of $\mathbb C^2$. $\square$

text: Definition 6.49.3 . 54F98147B130 For $j\geq 1$ set \[  \varepsilon _ j=\frac14\exp (-8^{j-1}),\qquad c_ j=\prod _{k=1}^ j\varepsilon _ k =4^{-j}\exp \! \left(-\frac{8^ j-1}{7}\right),  \] and define on $\mathbb C^2$ \[  H_ j=F_{\varepsilon _ j}\circ \cdots \circ F_{\varepsilon _1},\qquad p_ j=2^{-j}\log \| H_ j\| _\infty ^2,\qquad p_ j(0)=-\infty .  \] Write $e_2=(0,1)$.

text: Proposition 6.49.4 . DDF1EA12A4BF Each $p_ j$ is negative psh on the unit bidisc, continuous off zero, and tends to $-\infty $ at zero. In the normalization $\nu (v,0)=\liminf _{\zeta \to 0}v(\zeta )/\log \| \zeta \| ^2$, it satisfies \[  \nu (p_ j,0)=2^{-j},\qquad (dd^ cp_ j)^2=\delta _0.  \] Every finite sublevel of $p_ j$ is relatively compact in $\mathbb C^2$. Moreover \[  dH_ j(0)e_2=c_ je_2,\qquad \| H_ j(te_2)\| _\infty \geq c_ jt\quad (0<t<1).  \] Proof. The preceding corollary and homogeneity give $(dd^ cp_ j)^2=2^{-2j}4^ j\delta _0=\delta _0$ on $\mathbb C^2$. For $r=\| (z,w)\| _\infty \leq 1$ and $0<\varepsilon \leq 1/4$, \[  \| F_\varepsilon (z,w)\| _\infty \leq \tfrac 12r^2+\tfrac 14r\leq \tfrac 34.  \] Thus each map takes the unit bidisc into itself. The maximum of the two holomorphic component logarithms is plurisubharmonic. The zero-fiber statement gives the continuity and pole assertions. Closed finite sublevels of $p_ j$ are inverse images under the globally proper $H_ j$ of compact closed bidiscs, so they are compact. At zero $dF_\varepsilon =\operatorname {diag}(0,\varepsilon )$, so the chain rule proves the derivative formula. Along $(0,t)$ write $H_ k(0,t)=(z_ k,w_ k)$, with $(z_0,w_0)=(0,t)$. The recursion \[  z_ k=w_{k-1}^2/2,\qquad w_ k=z_{k-1}^2/2+\varepsilon _ kw_{k-1}  \] keeps both coordinates nonnegative and gives $w_ k\geq \varepsilon _ kw_{k-1}$, proving the last bound. Since $H_ j$ is holomorphic and vanishes at zero, a derivative bound on a small ball gives $\| H_ j(\zeta )\| _\infty \leq C_ j\| \zeta \| $. Dividing the resulting upper bound for $p_ j$ by the negative $\log \| \zeta \| ^2$ gives a lower limit at least $2^{-j}$. On the line $\zeta =te_2$, the derivative formula gives $H_ j(te_2)=c_ jte_2+O(t^2)$, so that the ratio tends to $2^{-j}$ there. The logarithmic characterization of the Lelong number, Lelong numbers as logarithmic growth slopes , proves the equality. Changing between the Euclidean and maximum norm adds a bounded term to the denominator and does not change this limit. $\square$

All products at an isolated pole in this section are the classical products of the theorem on classical products with compact unbounded loci . They include any mass at the pole. Write $\mathbb D^2$ for the unit bidisc and $\| \zeta \| _\infty =\max \{ |z|,|w|\} $ for $\zeta =(z,w)$. Let $F_\varepsilon $, $\varepsilon _ j$, $H_ j$ and $p_ j$ be the maps, parameters, iterates and weights of definition 6.49.3 . In particular, $p_ j<0$ on $\overline{\mathbb D^2}$, its only pole is zero, and $e^{p_ j}$ is continuous there. Put E147430C1211 6.50.1  egin{equation}  M_ j=2\cdot 4^ j,\qquad W_ j=\max \{ p_ j,-M_ j\} ,\qquad K_ j=\{ \zeta \in \overline{\mathbb D^2}:p_ j(\zeta )\leq -M_ j\} . \end{equation} Lemma 6.50.2 . 9D91DC8AF289 For $0<\varepsilon \leq 1/4$ and $\| \zeta \| _\infty \leq 1$, \[  \| F_\varepsilon (\zeta )\| _\infty \geq  rac18\| \zeta \| _\infty ^4.  \] Consequently 2BCC4F872AFE 6.50.3  egin{equation}  p_ j(\zeta )\geq 2^{j+1}\log \| \zeta \| _\infty -2(\log 2)(2^ j-2^{-j}). \end{equation} Each $K_ j$ contains a neighborhood of zero, is compactly contained in $\mathbb D^2$, and satisfies E8FFA55A2EB8 6.50.4  egin{equation}  K_ j\subset \{ \| \zeta \| _\infty \leq 2e^{-2^ j}\} . \end{equation} Proof. Set $r=\max \{ |z|,|w|\} $. If $|w|\geq r^2/2$, the first component of $F_\varepsilon $ has modulus at least $r^4/8$. If $|w|<r^2/2$, then $r>0$ and $r=|z|$, since $r\leq 1$. The second component has modulus at least \[   rac12r^2-\varepsilon |w|>  rac12r^2- rac18r^2= rac38r^2\geq  rac18r^4.  \] This proves the estimate; at zero it holds directly. Every iterate stays in the closed bidisc. Iterating the estimate therefore gives \[  \| H_ j(\zeta )\| _\infty \geq 8^{-(1+4+\cdots +4^{j-1})}\| \zeta \| _\infty ^{4^ j} =2^{1-4^ j}\| \zeta \| _\infty ^{4^ j}.  \] Taking $2^{-j}$ times the logarithm of its square proves ( 6.50.3 ). If $\zeta \in K_ j\setminus \{ 0\} $, this bound implies \[  \log \| \zeta \| _\infty \leq -2^ j+(\log 2)(1-4^{-j})\leq -2^ j+\log 2,  \] which proves ( 6.50.4 ), including zero. The function $e^{p_ j}$ is continuous on the closed bidisc and vanishes at zero. Its sublevel at the positive number $e^{-M_ j}$ is closed and contains a neighborhood of zero. Finally, $2e^{-2}<1$, so the displayed radius bound places this closed set inside a compact subset of the open bidisc. $\square$ Lemma 6.50.5 . EA0EF7A5BB47 For every $j\geq 1$, E3DD353DBBC8 6.50.6  egin{equation}  -2^{1-j}\log 2\leq p_{j+1}-p_ j\leq 0 \quad \hbox{on }\{ p_ j\geq -M_ j\} . \end{equation} On the whole bidisc, $p_{j+1}\leq W_ j$ and $W_{j+1}\leq W_ j$. Proof. Fix a nonzero point and write $H_ j(\zeta )=(z,w)$ and $r=\max \{ |z|,|w|\} >0$. Directly from the definition, 0394B9F53F55 6.50.7  egin{equation}  p_{j+1}(\zeta )-p_ j(\zeta ) =2^{-j}\log  rac{\| F_{\varepsilon _{j+1}}(z,w)\| _\infty }{r^2}. \end{equation} On the indicated set, $r\geq e^{-8^ j}$ and hence $\varepsilon _{j+1}=e^{-8^ j}/4\leq r/4$. The two components of $F_{\varepsilon _{j+1}}(z,w)$ have moduli at most $r^2/2$ and $3r^2/4$. If $r=|w|$, the first component has modulus $r^2/2$; if $r=|z|$, the second has modulus at least $r^2/2-\varepsilon _{j+1}r\geq r^2/4$. Thus the ratio in ( 6.50.7 ) belongs to $[1/4,1]$. This proves ( 6.50.6 ), and in particular $p_{j+1}\leq W_ j$ there. If $p_ j(\zeta )<-M_ j$, put $R_ j=e^{-8^ j}$ and $r=R_ jx$, where $0<x<1$. Then \[  \| F_{\varepsilon _{j+1}}(z,w)\| _\infty \leq R_ j^2\left( rac{x^2}{2}+ rac{x}{4}ight) <R_ j^2.  \] It follows that $p_{j+1}(\zeta )<-2\cdot 4^ j=-M_ j=W_ j(\zeta )$. At zero, $p_{j+1}(0)=-\infty $, so the global assertion holds there as well. Finally $-M_{j+1}\leq -M_ j\leq W_ j$; taking the maximum with $p_{j+1}$ proves $W_{j+1}\leq W_ j$. $\square$ Proposition 6.50.8 . 4058F9C6D2AC The bounded negative plurisubharmonic functions $W_ j$ decrease to a negative plurisubharmonic function $U$ on $\mathbb D^2$. Its pole set is $\{ 0\} $, it is continuous outside zero, and $e^ U$ is continuous on the whole bidisc. Both $p_ j$ and $W_ j$ converge locally uniformly to $U$ on the punctured bidisc. Proof. Each $W_ j$ is bounded and plurisubharmonic by closure under finite maxima for plurisubharmonic functions , and is strictly negative. The preceding lemma proves decreasing convergence to the extended-valued function $U=\inf _ jW_ j$. Let $L$ be a compact subset of the punctured bidisc. The radius bound ( 6.50.4 ) supplies $N$ such that $L\cap K_ k=\varnothing $ for every $k\geq N$. For $\ell >k\geq N$, the visible comparison gives \[  0\leq p_ k-p_\ell \leq \sum _{s=k}^{\ell -1}2^{1-s}\log 2 \leq 2^{2-k}\log 2\qquad \hbox{on }L.  \] Thus the finite continuous functions $p_ j$ are uniformly Cauchy on $L$. For $j\geq N$, $W_ j=p_ j$ there. Their common limit is finite and continuous on $L$. The decreasing-limit theorem for plurisubharmonic functions therefore applies with the identically $-\infty $ alternative excluded. Thus $U$ is plurisubharmonic and $U\leq W_1<0$. Since $W_ j(0)=-M_ j	o -\infty $, its pole set is exactly zero. For any $A>0$, choose $j$ with $M_ j>A$. The set $K_ j$ contains a neighborhood of zero, on which $U\leq W_ j=-M_ j<-A$. Therefore $U(\zeta )	o -\infty $ as $\zeta 	o 0$, proving continuity of $e^ U$ at zero and hence on the whole bidisc. $\square$ Lemma 6.50.9 . 1D1AC8862EEA If $p_ j(\zeta )>-M_ j$, then $p_ k(\zeta )>-M_ k$ for every $k\geq j$ and EA1C01079C02 6.50.10  egin{equation}  0\leq p_ j(\zeta )-U(\zeta )\leq 2^{2-j}\log 2. \end{equation} Proof. The visible comparison implies \[  p_{k+1}(\zeta )>-M_ k-2^{1-k}\log 2>-M_{k+1}  \] whenever $p_ k(\zeta )>-M_ k$. The last inequality holds for $k\geq 1$, since $M_{k+1}-M_ k=6\cdot 4^ k$ and $2^{1-k}\log 2\leq \log 2$. Induction proves that every later cutoff is inactive. Summing ( 6.50.6 ) from $j$ to $m-1$ and letting $m	o \infty $ proves ( 6.50.10 ). $\square$ Theorem 6.50.11 . 367D36FB36A0 The explicit function \[  U(\zeta )=\lim _{j	o \infty } \max \{ 2^{-j}\log \| H_ j(\zeta )\| _\infty ^2,-2\cdot 4^ j\}   \] is negative and plurisubharmonic on $\mathbb D^2$ and satisfies FC2BE4EE5D1B 6.50.12  egin{equation}  U^{-1}(-\infty )=\{ 0\} ,\qquad e^ U\in C^0(\mathbb D^2),\qquad 
u (U,0)=0,\qquad (dd^ cU)^2=\delta _0. \end{equation} Proof. The assertions about its sign, pole set and continuity follow from proposition 6.50.8 . The mass. By proposition 6.49.4 , $(dd^ cp_ j)^2=\delta _0$. On the boundary of the bidisc, ( 6.50.3 ) gives \[  p_ j\geq -2(\log 2)(2^ j-2^{-j})>-M_ j.  \] Since $p_ j$ is continuous near that compact boundary, choose $s_ j$ strictly between $-M_ j$ and the boundary minimum. Then $\{ p_ j<s_ j\} $ is relatively compact in $\mathbb D^2$. The weight $p_ j$ is extended-continuous, with its only pole at zero. The bidisc admits the smooth strictly plurisubharmonic exhaustion $-\log (1-|z|^2)-\log (1-|w|^2)$. Apply the swept boundary measure formula at level $-M_ j$. Its restriction term $\mathbf1_{\{ p_ j\geq -M_ j\} }(dd^ cp_ j)^2$ vanishes. Hence $(dd^ cW_ j)^2$ is a probability measure supported on $\{ p_ j=-M_ j\} \subset K_ j$. For every $\chi \in C_ c(\mathbb D^2)$, \[  \left|\int \chi (dd^ cW_ j)^2-\chi (0)ight| \leq \sup _{K_ j}|\chi -\chi (0)|\longrightarrow 0,  \] by ( 6.50.4 ). The classical continuity theorem cited at the start applies to $W_ j\downarrow U$: every point admits a coordinate ball whose boundary avoids the isolated pole, and all these functions are locally bounded on its boundary collar. It follows that $(dd^ cW_ j)^2$ also converges to $(dd^ cU)^2$. The two weak limits give $(dd^ cU)^2=\delta _0$. The Lelong number. Let $e_2=(0,1)$ and \[  c_ j=4^{-j}\exp \left(- rac{8^ j-1}{7}ight),\qquad L_ j=-\log c_ j=j\log 4+ rac{8^ j-1}{7},\qquad \zeta _ j=c_ je_2.  \] The positive-ray estimate for the iterates gives $\| H_ j(\zeta _ j)\| _\infty \geq c_ j^2$. Thus $B_ j=-p_ j(\zeta _ j)$ satisfies \[  0\leq B_ j\leq 2^{2-j}L_ j, \qquad  rac{2^{2-j}L_ j}{M_ j}\longrightarrow  rac27<1.  \] For all sufficiently large $j$ the point $\zeta _ j$ is therefore in the visible set $\{ p_ j>-M_ j\} $. The tail estimate gives \[  U(\zeta _ j)\geq -B_ j-2^{2-j}\log 2.  \] Since $U\leq 0$ and $\log \| \zeta _ j\| _\infty ^2=-2L_ j<0$, \[  0\leq  rac{U(\zeta _ j)}{\log \| \zeta _ j\| _\infty ^2} \leq 2^{1-j}+ rac{2^{1-j}\log 2}{L_ j}\longrightarrow 0.  \] Finally $c_ j	o 0$. The logarithmic growth characterization of the Lelong number identifies $
u (U,0)$ with the lower limit of the quotient in the last display. Indeed, its spherical-supremum formulation gives this lower limit by choosing a point attaining the supremum on each small sphere. Replacing the Euclidean norm by the maximum norm changes its logarithm by a bounded amount. The resulting nonnegative lower limit is zero along $\zeta _ j$, so $
u (U,0)=0$. $\square$

text: We use $dd^ c=\frac{i}{2\pi }\partial \bar\partial $ and the classical Bedford–Taylor products. In particular, the products at an isolated pole include their mass at that pole. Lemma 7.33.1 . 11B8D65C2D19 Let $f,g$ be locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions on an open subset of $\mathbb C^ N$, put $h=\max \{ f,g\} $, and write $A=dd^ cf$, $B=dd^ cg$, and $C=dd^ ch$. For $1\leq k\leq N$, 32CB78FC0E95 7.33.2 \begin{equation}  C^ k=C\wedge \sum _{j=0}^{k-1}A^ j\wedge B^{k-1-j} -\sum _{j=1}^{k-1}A^ j\wedge B^{k-j}. \end{equation} The second sum is zero when $k=1$. Proof. All products and scalar weights below are the bounded recursive products , with their symmetry . By maximum locality , $C^ k=B^ k$ on the Borel set $\{ g>f\} $ in the sense of restriction of coefficient measures. The locally bounded nonnegative function $h-f$ vanishes on its complement. Hence \[  (h-f)C^ k=(h-f)B^ k.  \] Apply $dd^ c$. The recursive definition and symmetry give, for $1\leq k<N$, \[  C^{k+1}-A\wedge C^ k=C\wedge B^ k-A\wedge B^ k.  \] Starting with $C^1=C$, this recurrence proves ( 7.33.2 ) by induction: multiplication of the $k$th identity by $A$, followed by addition of $C\wedge B^ k-A\wedge B^ k$, gives exactly the $(k+1)$st identity. Every scalar multiplication used here is multiplication of the coefficient measures of a bounded product; no multiplication of distributions is required. $\square$ Theorem 7.33.3 . F8604F30C7C6 Let $D\subset \mathbb C^ p$ and $G\subset \mathbb C^ q$ be open, where $p,q\geq 1$. Suppose that $f\geq 0$ and $g\geq 0$ are plurisubharmonic on $D$ and $G$, respectively, and \[  \mathbf1_{\{ f>0\} }(dd^ cf)^ p=0, \qquad \mathbf1_{\{ g>0\} }(dd^ cg)^ q=0.  \] Then, on $D\times G$, BD9883DFED0B 7.33.4 \begin{equation}  \bigl (dd^ c\max \{ f(z),g(w)\} \bigr )^{p+q} =(dd^ cf)^ p\otimes (dd^ cg)^ q. \end{equation} The right-hand side is the product measure, with no binomial factor. Proof. The nonnegative plurisubharmonic functions are locally bounded: upper semicontinuity bounds them above on compact neighborhoods, and zero is a lower bound. Put $h(z,w)=\max \{ f(z),g(w)\} $, and let $A,B,C$ denote the pulled-back Hessians of $f,g$ and the Hessian of $h$, as in the preceding lemma. For $0\leq a\leq p$ and $0\leq b\leq q$, products of these separate-variable Hessians satisfy \[  A^ a\wedge B^ b=(dd^ cf)^ a\otimes (dd^ cg)^ b.  \] Indeed, regularize $f$ and $g$ decreasingly on relatively compact coordinate domains in their own variables. For smooth potentials the formula is ordinary exterior algebra and Fubini. Bounded decreasing continuity passes the left-hand side to its limit. On the right, the coefficient measures have locally uniformly bounded total variations, by positivity and their trace masses. Their tensor products converge: for a smooth compact test coefficient $F(z,w)$, a finite smooth partition in the $z$ variables approximates it uniformly on a containing compact rectangle by finite sums $\sum _ i\rho _ i(z)F(z_ i,w)$, with fixed compact cutoffs in both factors. Each separated term converges by the two weak convergences; the uniform total-variation bound controls the approximation error. This proves the displayed tensor identity. The same smooth approximation proves $A^{p+1}=B^{q+1}=0$ by degree. Apply ( 7.33.2 ) with $k=p+q$. Only two terms in the first sum and one in the second can survive: 5E25FA94CA28 7.33.5 \begin{equation}  C^{p+q} =C\wedge \bigl (A^{p-1}\wedge B^ q+A^ p\wedge B^{q-1}\bigr ) -A^ p\wedge B^ q. \end{equation} The coefficient measures of $S=A^{p-1}\wedge B^ q$ give zero mass to $D\times \{ g>0\} $, by the tensor identity and the hypothesis on $(dd^ cg)^ q$. On the complementary set $g=0$, nonnegativity of $f$ gives $h=f$. Thus $hS=fS$ as weighted currents, and bounded recursion gives \[  C\wedge A^{p-1}\wedge B^ q =dd^ c(hS)=dd^ c(fS)=A^ p\wedge B^ q.  \] Interchanging the factors similarly gives $C\wedge A^ p\wedge B^{q-1}=A^ p\wedge B^ q$. Substitution in ( 7.33.5 ) leaves one copy of $A^ p\wedge B^ q$, proving the assertion. $\square$

Corollary 6.50.14 . ECF3A574075A For every $n\geq 2$ there is a negative plurisubharmonic function $U_ n$ on the unit polydisc $\mathbb D^ n$ whose unbounded locus is $\{ 0\} $, such that $e^{U_ n}$ is continuous, \[  
u (U_ n,0)=0, \qquad (dd^ cU_ n)^ n=\delta _0.  \] The Monge–Ampère measure here is the classical measure at the isolated pole. Proof. Let $U$ be the two-dimensional function of theorem 6.50.11 . This proves the case $n=2$. For $n>2$ put $m=n-2$, write coordinates as $(z,w)$, and set \[  V(w)=\log \| w\| _\infty ^2=\max _{1\leq j\leq m}\log |w_ j|^2, \qquad U_ n(z,w)=\max \{ U(z),V(w)\} .  \] The function $V$ is negative plurisubharmonic with its only pole at zero, and $(dd^ cV)^ m=\delta _0$ by the anisotropic logarithmic-pole formula . Moreover, \[  e^{U_ n(z,w)}=\max \{ e^{U(z)},\| w\| _\infty ^2\} .  \] This is continuous and vanishes only at $(0,0)$; consequently $U_ n$ is finite and locally bounded away from that point. It is negative and plurisubharmonic by holomorphic pullback and the maximum operation. If $a=
u (U_ n,0)$, the attained logarithmic growth bound restricts on $w=0$ to $U(z)\leq a\log |z|^2+O(1)$. The same growth characterization gives $0=
u (U,0)\geq a\geq 0$. Fix $0<r<1$ and work on $\Omega _1=r\mathbb D^2$ and $\Omega _2=r\mathbb D^ m$. Both potentials are continuous and finite on neighborhoods of their respective boundaries, so their sufficiently low closed sublevels are compact in those domains. For all sufficiently large $T$ put \[  f_ T=\max \{ U,-2T\} +2T, \qquad g_ T=\max \{ V,-2T\} +2T.  \] The boundary sweeping formula applies to these extended-continuous weights on the polydiscs, which admit the smooth strictly plurisubharmonic exhaustions $-\sum _ j\log (r^2-|z_ j|^2)$ and $-\sum _ j\log (r^2-|w_ j|^2)$. Since the original classical measures are unit point masses at their poles, it gives probability measures \[   egin{gathered} (dd^ cf_ T)^2	ext{ supported on }\{ U=-2T\} \subset \{ f_ T=0\} , \ (dd^ cg_ T)^ m	ext{ supported on }\{ V=-2T\} \subset \{ g_ T=0\} . \end{gathered}  \] The preceding theorem therefore gives \[   igl (dd^ c\max \{ U_ n,-2T\}  igr )^ n =(dd^ cf_ T)^2\otimes (dd^ cg_ T)^ m,  \] because $\max \{ f_ T,g_ T\} =\max \{ U_ n,-2T\} +2T$. These product probability measures have supports contained in $\{ U\leq -2T\} 	imes \{ V\leq -2T\} $, which shrink to $(0,0)$. Indeed, on any compact set separated from the respective origin, the continuous functions $e^ U$ and $e^ V$ have a positive minimum; the low sublevels already lie in a fixed compact subset of each domain. The product measures consequently tend weakly to $\delta _0$. Finally, $\max \{ U_ n,-2T\} \downarrow U_ n$. The classical decreasing-continuity theorem applies in every dimension: near the isolated unbounded point one chooses a coordinate ball whose boundary avoids it, and outside that point the potentials are locally bounded. It identifies the last weak limit with $(dd^ cU_ n)^ n$ on $r\mathbb D^ n$. As $r<1$ was arbitrary, this proves the formula on $\mathbb D^ n$. $\square$

Use $dd^ c=\mathrm i\partial  ar\partial /(2\pi )$ and $\ell (z)=\log |z|^2$, so $(dd^ c\ell )^ N=\delta _0$ on $\mathbb C^ N$. All products below are the classical products, retaining the pole mass. An isolated unbounded locus satisfies the common-boundary hypothesis in the theorem on classical products with compact unbounded loci . In particular all mixed products used below are locally finite and their decreasing bounded truncations converge, including at the origin. Lemma 6.51.1 . BE4AE95DA940 Let $N\geq 2$ and let $a,b$ be plurisubharmonic near $0\in \mathbb C^ N$, locally bounded away from zero. Set \[  m_ j= igl ((dd^ ca)^ j\wedge (dd^ cb)^{N-j} igr )(\{ 0\} ), \qquad 0\leq j\leq N.  \] Then $m_ j$ are finite and nonnegative, and \[  m_ j^2\leq m_{j-1}m_{j+1},\qquad 1\leq j<N.  \] Proof. We first explain the boundary reduction. After a coordinate dilation, choose two concentric spheres inside a ball on which both germs are defined. A radial function $A\ell $ with $A>0$ sufficiently large and a suitable additive shift of $a$ satisfy $A\ell <a$ on a neighborhood of the inner sphere and $A\ell >a$ on a neighborhood of the outer sphere. Indeed the two compact annuli have finite upper and lower bounds for $a$, and the difference of the two radial values grows linearly with $A$. Retain $a$ inside the inner sphere, use $\max \{ a,A\ell \} $ between the spheres, and retain $A\ell $ outside the outer sphere. Strict inequalities on the overlap collars make this a plurisubharmonic function on a neighborhood of the closed unit ball. Subtracting the boundary constant, if necessary, makes it equal to $A\ell $ near the unit sphere. Do this separately for $b$. The new functions have the same germs up to constants and coordinate dilation, which do not change their residual mixed masses. Write them again as $a,b$. They are negative on the unit ball and vanish at its boundary. Here is the required weighted Cauchy–Schwarz argument, with its boundary and approximation details. Suppose first that $a,b,h$ are smooth plurisubharmonic functions on the closed unit ball, vanish at its boundary, and $h\leq 0$. For a closed positive smooth current $T$ of bidegree $(N-2,N-2)$, define \[  B_ T(f,g)=\int _{B_1}(-h)\, dd^ cf\wedge dd^ cg\wedge T  \] for smooth real $f,g$ vanishing at the boundary. Two integrations by parts, whose boundary terms contain $h$ or $f$, give \[  B_ T(f,f)=\int _{B_1}(-f)\, dd^ ch\wedge dd^ cf\wedge T =\int _{B_1}df\wedge d^ cf\wedge dd^ ch\wedge T\geq 0.  \] Thus the real symmetric bilinear form $B_ T$ is positive semidefinite. The discriminant of $B_ T(a+tb,a+tb)\geq 0$ gives BE95E4FF4E8F 6.51.2  egin{equation}  \left(\int (-h)\, dd^ ca\wedge dd^ cb\wedge Tight)^2 \leq \left(\int (-h)(dd^ ca)^2\wedge Tight) \left(\int (-h)(dd^ cb)^2\wedge Tight). \end{equation} For $N=2$ take $T=1$. For $N>2$, take $T=(dd^ ca)^{j-1}\wedge (dd^ cb)^{N-j-1}$. We justify this argument for the bounded truncations of our patched germs. Put $a_ k=\max \{ a,-k\} $ and $b_ k=\max \{ b,-k\} $, for all sufficiently large $k$; both have the fixed radial collars above. For an integer $l\geq 1$, put \[  h_ l=\max \{ \ell /l,-1\} .  \] All three bounded functions extend plurisubharmonically beyond the closed unit ball. Convolve with a radial nonnegative smooth kernel of radius $\varepsilon $. Near the unit sphere the convolutions are radial, hence constant on that sphere. Subtract that constant from each convolution. This produces smooth plurisubharmonic functions with zero boundary values, so the preceding inequality applies. The constants tend to zero. Convolution before this constant shift decreases to each bounded potential as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$; the shifts do not change any Hessian factor. The weight $h_ l$ is continuous, so its convolutions and boundary shifts converge uniformly. By the decreasing-continuity theorem for bounded Bedford–Taylor products , all integrals therefore pass to the limit on compact subsets. There is no lost boundary contribution in this passage. On a fixed outer collar all Hessians of the convolutions are uniformly bounded. Stokes, applied to their smooth mixed top products, expresses the total mixed mass by a boundary integral of their first and second derivatives, which are uniformly bounded on that collar. Hence these total masses are uniformly bounded. Since the weights converge uniformly to $h_ l$, which vanishes on the boundary, their integrals on a sufficiently thin boundary collar are uniformly small. This passes ( 6.51.2 ) to $a_ k,b_ k,h_ l$. Now let $k	o \infty $. Classical mixed-product continuity applies by the theorem on classical products with compact unbounded loci . The same fixed radial collars give a uniform bound for the total mixed masses, independently of $k$, by the preceding smooth Stokes argument. title: Lemma 6.51.1
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
text: Lemma 6.51.1 . BE4AE95DA940 Let $N\geq 2$ and let $a,b$ be plurisubharmonic near $0\in \mathbb C^ N$, locally bounded away from zero. Set \[  m_ j=\bigl ((dd^ ca)^ j\wedge (dd^ cb)^{N-j}\bigr )(\{ 0\} ), \qquad 0\leq j\leq N.  \] Then $m_ j$ are finite and nonnegative, and \[  m_ j^2\leq m_{j-1}m_{j+1},\qquad 1\leq j<N.  \] Proof. We first explain the boundary reduction. After a coordinate dilation, choose two concentric spheres inside a ball on which both germs are defined. A radial function $A\ell $ with $A>0$ sufficiently large and a suitable additive shift of $a$ satisfy $A\ell <a$ on a neighborhood of the inner sphere and $A\ell >a$ on a neighborhood of the outer sphere. Indeed the two compact annuli have finite upper and lower bounds for $a$, and the difference of the two radial values grows linearly with $A$. Retain $a$ inside the inner sphere, use $\max \{ a,A\ell \} $ between the spheres, and retain $A\ell $ outside the outer sphere. Strict inequalities on the overlap collars make this a plurisubharmonic function on a neighborhood of the closed unit ball. Subtracting the boundary constant, if necessary, makes it equal to $A\ell $ near the unit sphere. Do this separately for $b$. The new functions have the same germs up to constants and coordinate dilation, which do not change their residual mixed masses. Write them again as $a,b$. They are negative on the unit ball and vanish at its boundary. Here is the required weighted Cauchy–Schwarz argument, with its boundary and approximation details. Suppose first that $a,b,h$ are smooth plurisubharmonic functions on the closed unit ball, vanish at its boundary, and $h\leq 0$. For a closed positive smooth current $T$ of bidegree $(N-2,N-2)$, define \[  B_ T(f,g)=\int _{B_1}(-h)\, dd^ cf\wedge dd^ cg\wedge T  \] for smooth real $f,g$ vanishing at the boundary. Two integrations by parts, whose boundary terms contain $h$ or $f$, give \[  B_ T(f,f)=\int _{B_1}(-f)\, dd^ ch\wedge dd^ cf\wedge T =\int _{B_1}df\wedge d^ cf\wedge dd^ ch\wedge T\geq 0.  \] Thus the real symmetric bilinear form $B_ T$ is positive semidefinite. The discriminant of $B_ T(a+tb,a+tb)\geq 0$ gives BE95E4FF4E8F 6.51.2 \begin{equation}  \left(\int (-h)\, dd^ ca\wedge dd^ cb\wedge T\right)^2 \leq \left(\int (-h)(dd^ ca)^2\wedge T\right) \left(\int (-h)(dd^ cb)^2\wedge T\right). \end{equation} For $N=2$ take $T=1$. For $N>2$, take $T=(dd^ ca)^{j-1}\wedge (dd^ cb)^{N-j-1}$. We justify this argument for the bounded truncations of our patched germs. Put $a_ k=\max \{ a,-k\} $ and $b_ k=\max \{ b,-k\} $, for all sufficiently large $k$; both have the fixed radial collars above. For an integer $l\geq 1$, put \[  h_ l=\max \{ \ell /l,-1\} .  \] All three bounded functions extend plurisubharmonically beyond the closed unit ball. Convolve with a radial nonnegative smooth kernel of radius $\varepsilon $. Near the unit sphere the convolutions are radial, hence constant on that sphere. Subtract that constant from each convolution. This produces smooth plurisubharmonic functions with zero boundary values, so the preceding inequality applies. The constants tend to zero. Convolution before this constant shift decreases to each bounded potential as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$; the shifts do not change any Hessian factor. The weight $h_ l$ is continuous, so its convolutions and boundary shifts converge uniformly. By the decreasing-continuity theorem for bounded Bedford–Taylor products , all integrals therefore pass to the limit on compact subsets. There is no lost boundary contribution in this passage. On a fixed outer collar all Hessians of the convolutions are uniformly bounded. Stokes, applied to their smooth mixed top products, expresses the total mixed mass by a boundary integral of their first and second derivatives, which are uniformly bounded on that collar. Hence these total masses are uniformly bounded. Since the weights converge uniformly to $h_ l$, which vanishes on the boundary, their integrals on a sufficiently thin boundary collar are uniformly small. This passes ( 6.51.2 ) to $a_ k,b_ k,h_ l$. Now let $k\to \infty $. Classical mixed-product continuity applies by the theorem on classical products with compact unbounded loci . The same fixed radial collars give a uniform bound for the total mixed masses, independently of $k$, by the preceding smooth Stokes argument. Thus the continuous weight $h_ l$, zero at the boundary, permits the same passage to the limit for the whole-ball integrals. Finally $-h_ l$ is bounded by one and tends pointwise to $1_{\{ 0\} }$. Dominated convergence for each finite mixed measure proves the stated residual inequality. $\square$

title: 6.51.8 Asymmetry of an isolated pole

text: Corollary 6.51.9 . 2B4173DC2F80 The explicit potential $U$ of theorem 6.50.11 is not invariant under simultaneous circular rotations. It is not uniformly directional Lipschitz near zero, in the sense that $r\partial _ rU$ cannot be essentially bounded on any punctured neighborhood. Its logarithmic truncation threshold is infinite. Proof. The last assertion follows from theorem 6.51.6 : this potential has zero Lelong number and positive residual mass. The radial proposition then excludes uniform directional Lipschitz continuity. There is also a direct numerical witness for the failure of circular invariance. Use the iterates and $p_ j$ of definition 6.49.3 . Put \[  \varepsilon _1=\frac1{4e},\qquad \zeta =\left(\mathrm i\sqrt{\varepsilon _1/16},\frac1{32}\right).  \] Both $\zeta $ and $\mathrm i\zeta $ lie in the unit bidisc. Direct substitution in $H_1=F_{\varepsilon _1}$ gives \[  \| H_1(\zeta )\| _\infty =\frac1{2048},\qquad \| H_1(\mathrm i\zeta )\| _\infty =\frac{\sqrt2\varepsilon _1}{32}.  \] The ratio of the latter to the former is $16\sqrt2/e>4$. Moreover $p_1(\zeta )=-11\log 2>-8$, and the rotated point has a larger $p_1$ value. The visible-tail estimate lemma 6.50.9 , at $j=1$, therefore gives \[  U(\mathrm i\zeta )\geq p_1(\mathrm i\zeta )-2\log 2 >p_1(\zeta )\geq U(\zeta ).  \] This proves noninvariance directly from the construction, without using a symmetry-case zero-mass theorem. $\square$

Ambient manifolds are connected unless stated otherwise. Fibers need not be connected; the section-envelope arguments treat their connected components separately. We use $dd^ c=\mathrm i\partial  ar\partial /(2\pi )$ and $
u (\log |z|^2,0)=1$. A restriction of a positive $(1,1)$-current to a connected complex submanifold means restriction of its local plurisubharmonic potentials; it is defined when those restrictions are not identically $-\infty $. For a plurisubharmonic $u$ near $0\in \mathbb C^ n$, use the circular mean \[  m_ u(r_1,\ldots ,r_ n)= rac1{(2\pi )^ n} \int _{[0,2\pi ]^ n}u(r_1e^{it_1},\ldots ,r_ ne^{it_ n})\, \mathrm dt  \] The existing directional mean and supremum theorem , with every directional weight equal to one, identifies its diagonal logarithmic slope with $
u (u,0)$. Coordinatewise monotonicity follows by the one-variable submean inequality. We use that canonical result without repeating its statement or proof. Proposition 6.52.1 . 3948CB675433 Let $\pi :\widehat X	o X$ be the blowup of a smooth complex submanifold. For every closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T$ and $\widehat x\in \widehat X$, \[  
u (T,\pi (\widehat x))\leq 
u (\pi ^*T,\widehat x) \leq 2
u (T,\pi (\widehat x)).  \] The factor two is uniform and no analytic-singularity assumption is required. Proof. Away from the exceptional divisor the map is a biholomorphism. At an exceptional point, a linear change of normal coordinates aligns that point's normal direction with the first coordinate. In centered coordinates the blowup map is \[  (t,u_2,\ldots ,u_ q,v)\longmapsto (t,tu_2,\ldots ,tu_ q,v),  \] where $q$ is the center's codimension. For $q=1$ it is the identity. Let $u$ be a local plurisubharmonic potential of $T$. It pulls back to a nondegenerate plurisubharmonic function, because the map has an open image off its exceptional set. The exponent matrix of the displayed monomial map has determinant one. Its map on the angular tori therefore preserves normalized Haar measure. The circular mean of $u\circ \pi $ with all source radii equal to $r$ is consequently \[  m_ u(r,r^2,\ldots ,r^2,r,\ldots ,r).  \] Every radius lies between $r^2$ and $r$ for $0<r<1$. Monotonicity and the cited diagonal mean formula, after division by $\log r^2<0$, give the two asserted bounds. Bounded smooth changes of potential do not affect the numbers. $\square$ Lemma 6.52.2 . 3C256C55C09B In the same setting, let $E$ be a component of the exceptional divisor, $\widehat T\geq 0$ a closed $(1,1)$-current, and $T=\pi _*\widehat T$. At $\widehat x\in E$, away from other exceptional components, one has \[  
u (\widehat T,\widehat x)-
u (\widehat T,E) \leq 2
u (T,\pi (\widehat x)).  \] Here a smooth connected center has only one exceptional component. Proof. The two currents $\pi ^*T$ and $\widehat T$ agree off the exceptional divisor. The support theorem for closed currents of order zero makes their difference a constant multiple of $[E]$. Set $a=
u (\widehat T,E)$ and $b=
u (\pi ^*T,E)$. Their positive divisorial residuals therefore agree: \[  \widehat T-a[E]=\pi ^*T-b[E]\geq 0.  \] Since $E$ is smooth, taking the Lelong number at $\widehat x$ subtracts exactly $a$, respectively $b$. The latter residual number is at most $
u (\pi ^*T,\widehat x)$, which is bounded by the preceding proposition. The support theorem used here is the support theorem for normal currents ; the positive divisorial residual follows from the single-divisor subtraction step in the proof of Siu's divisorial decomposition . That step is local near the smooth divisor and does not require the compactness assumed for the global decomposition. $\square$

title: 6.53 Projective-bundle integration
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
text:
Ambient manifolds are connected unless stated otherwise. Fibers need not be connected; the section-envelope arguments treat their connected components separately. Lemma 6.53.1 . 9F447047F3B1 For a plurisubharmonic function $u$ near the origin, its restriction to almost every complex line through the origin is defined and has Lelong number $
u (u,0)$. Proof. The logarithmic growth bound gives $
u (u|_ L,0)\geq 
u (u,0)$ whenever the restriction is defined. Subtract a constant so $u\leq 0$, and average first over the circles in complex lines and then over their invariant probability measure. Fubini identifies this with the spherical mean of $u$. Choose two radii at which these means are finite. For almost every line the circle means are finite there; their convexity in $\log r^2$ makes their nonnegative secant slopes, with the larger radius fixed, decrease as $r\downarrow 0$. They are dominated by the integrable secant slope at the second fixed radius. u (u,0)$ by the Jensen characterization of Lelong numbers . Since each limiting slope is at least that number, equality holds almost everywhere. $\square$ Corollary 6.53.2 . 3B59FC78B4DD For a smooth-center blowup and a plurisubharmonic $u$ downstairs, \[  \min _{\widehat x\in \pi ^{-1}(x)}
u (u\circ \pi ,\widehat x) =
u (u,x).  \] Proof. Every number on the left is at least the right-hand side by logarithmic growth. Choose a generic complex line through $x$ whose direction is transverse to the center. u (u,x)$ on the line. Restriction to the strict transform cannot decrease the ambient number upstairs, so that number is also at most $
u (u,x)$. $\square$ Proposition 6.53.3 . 1544E8213A91 Let $V$ be a rank $r\geq 1$ holomorphic vector bundle on a complex manifold, let $\pi :\mathbb P(V)	o X$ be its projective bundle, and let $\omega $ be a Kähler form on $\mathbb P(V)$. u (T',x)\geq v\, 
u (T,\pi ^{-1}(x)).  \] The number on the right is the generic, equivalently minimal, Lelong number along the smooth fiber. Proof. Local constancy of $v$ follows by integration of a closed form in a locally trivial proper smooth family. If $\dim X=1$, the fiber is a smooth divisor. Subtract its generic divisorial coefficient $a=
u (T,\pi ^{-1}(x))$ to obtain \[  T'\geq \pi _*(a[\pi ^{-1}(x)]\wedge \omega ^{r-1})=av[x].  \] Taking the atom proves the assertion. For higher-dimensional $X$, take a generic coordinate complex line disc $\Delta $ through $x$. The preceding lemma gives $
u (T'|_\Delta ,x)=
u (T',x)$. The restriction of $T$ to $\pi ^{-1}(\Delta )$ is defined for almost every such disc, and fiber integration commutes with this restriction. One can check this at the level of potentials, including the center of the disc. This representation follows by subtracting the constant fiber cohomology class; the remaining local potentials glue modulo pluriharmonic functions, since $H^1(U	imes \mathbb P^{r-1},\mathcal O)=0$ and its real degree-two cohomology is generated by the fiber hyperplane class. title: 10.102 Strictly positive singular metrics
text: Ambient manifolds are connected unless stated otherwise. Fibers need not be connected; the section-envelope arguments treat their connected components separately. Theorem 10.102.1 . 4F4355678C85 Let $(Z,\omega )$ be a compact Kähler manifold and $(B,h)$ a singular Hermitian line bundle. If $c_1(B,h)\geq \delta \omega $ for some $\delta >0$, then \[  H^ q(Z,K_ Z\otimes B\otimes \mathcal I(h))=0\quad (q\geq 1).  \] Here the multiplier ideal uses the full quadratic metric weight. Proof. Write $h=h_0e^{-\psi }$ with $h_0$ smooth and curvature $\theta $. Normalize $\psi \leq 0$. The existing strong openness theorem and compactness give a small rational $a>0$ such that $\mathcal I((1+a)\psi )=\mathcal I(\psi )$. For the decreasing quasi-equisingular analytic approximants $\psi _ j$, applied with background form $\theta -\delta \omega $, the two ideal inclusions give, for all large $j$, \[  \mathcal I(\psi )=\mathcal I((1+a)\psi ) \subset \mathcal I((1+a)\psi _ j)\subset \mathcal I(\psi ).  \] Choose $a$ small and then $j$ large. The curvature $\theta +(1+a)dd^ c\psi _ j$ is at least $\delta \omega /2$: it equals $(1+a)(\theta +dd^ c\psi _ j)-a\theta $ and the approximation error tends to zero. We can consequently replace $h$ by a gentle analytic-singularity metric with the same ideal and a strict positive lower bound. For completeness, the global $L^2$ step works as follows. Let $A$ be the analytic pole set. On $Z\setminus A$ the metric is smooth. If $A$ is empty use $\Omega =\omega $. Otherwise let $v$ be the replacement weight just constructed, shifted by a constant so that $v\leq -2$. It is smooth off $A$, tends to $-\infty $ at $A$, and satisfies $dd^ cv\geq -C\omega $. For sufficiently large fixed $C'$, the form $\Omega =C'\omega +dd^ c[-\log (-v)]$ is Kähler off $A$. Its gradient term $dv\wedge d^ cv/v^2$ makes every path approaching $A$ have infinite length, by the variation of $\log (-v)$. This gives the required complete metric. Use the complete metrics $\omega _ t=\omega +t\Omega $, $t>0$. Apply the existing complete Kähler inverse-curvature theorem in bidegree $(n,q)$, together with the bundle curvature operator formula . That theorem includes every $1\leq q\leq n$ and the required compactly supported approximation in the maximal operator domains. In an $\omega $-unitary frame diagonalizing $\omega _ t$, write its eigenvalues as $\lambda _ i\geq 1$. The curvature operator on a component with index set $J$, $|J|=q$, is bounded below by $(\delta /2)\sum _{i\in J}\lambda _ i^{-1}$. The ratio of its inverse energy density to the original $\omega $ square density is at most \[  \frac{\prod _{i\in J}\lambda _ i^{-1}}{(\delta /2)\sum _{i\in J}\lambda _ i^{-1}} \leq \frac{2}{q\delta }.  \] The last inequality follows by summing $q$ products of $q-1$ numbers at most one. Moreover the $\omega _ t$ square density of an $(n,q)$-form is its $\omega $ density multiplied componentwise by $\prod _{i\in J}\lambda _ i^{-1}\leq 1$; hence $g$ satisfies the theorem's global $L^2$ hypothesis for every $t>0$. Thus a closed square-integrable $g$ has solutions $\bar\partial u_ t=g$ whose squared $L^2(h,\omega _ t)$ norms are bounded by $2\| g\| _{h,\omega }^2/(q\delta )$. On every compact subset of $Z\setminus A$, the metrics $\omega _ t$ converge uniformly to $\omega $. A diagonal weakly convergent subsequence on a compact exhaustion gives a distributional solution as $t\downarrow 0$. Weak lower semicontinuity of the squared norm on each compact subset, followed by exhaustion, bounds its squared $\omega $-norm by $2\| g\| ^2/(q\delta )$. The coefficients of $u$ are locally unweighted $L^2$ as well, since the metric weights are bounded above. Extend them across $A$ as $L^2$ coefficients. The equation extends distributionally: use logarithmic cutoffs about the analytic set, whose gradient $L^2$ norm tends to zero, and Cauchy–Schwarz against the local $L^2$ coefficients. These are the same removable-set cutoffs used in the singular-weight $\bar\partial $ estimate. Finally take the sheaves of $B$-valued $(n,q)$-forms for which both the form and its distributional $\bar\partial $ are locally $L^2(h)$. Their kernel in degree zero is precisely $K_ Z\otimes B\otimes \mathcal I(h)$. Local exactness in positive degree follows on a ball from the singular-weight $\bar\partial $ estimate in degree one and, for $2\leq q\leq n$, the singular-weight higher-degree theorem . Adding a bounded strictly plurisubharmonic weight on the ball provides a positive curvature lower bound without changing the local weighted $L^2$ spaces. The sheaves are fine, since multiplication by a smooth cutoff preserves the local conditions. This gives a fine resolution. Compactness makes its global coefficients square-integrable, and the global solution just proved kills all its positive-degree cohomology. This proves the assertion. $\square$

title: 9.71 Local projectivity from relative positivity
text: Ambient manifolds are connected unless stated otherwise. Fibers need not be connected; the section-envelope arguments treat their connected components separately. Lemma 9.71.1 . A53CEC220C70 Let $p:M\to V$ be a proper holomorphic submersion of complex manifolds, and let $A$ be a holomorphic line bundle with a smooth metric whose curvature is positive on every fiber. Every point $y_0\in V$ has a neighborhood $U$, an integer $k>0$, and a closed holomorphic embedding over $U$ \[  G:M_ U\hookrightarrow \mathbb P^ N\times U, \qquad A^{\otimes k}|_{M_ U}=G^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ N}(1).  \] Proof. If $M_{y_0}$ is empty, properness gives a neighborhood with empty inverse image, and the assertion is immediate. Otherwise shrink to the image of the submersion. Choose a coordinate neighborhood of $y_0$ with compact closure. The inverse image of its closure is compact. The vertical curvature of $A$ defines a Kähler metric on every fiber. Give $K_{M/V}$ a smooth metric; its vertical curvature is bounded above by a fixed multiple of that of $A$ on this compact set. Thus, for one $k_0$ and every $k\geq k_0$, the vertical curvature of $A^{\otimes k}\otimes K_{M/V}^{-1}$ has a uniform strictly positive lower bound. Applying theorem 10.102.1 on each fiber, with this smooth metric and trivial multiplier ideal, gives \[  H^ q(M_ y,A_ y^{\otimes k})=0\qquad (q>0,\  k\geq k_0).  \] We use the following precise external analytic base-change input. For a proper holomorphic map to a reduced base and a coherent sheaf flat over it, the Euler characteristic of the fiber is locally constant; if its degree-zero cohomology dimension is constant, the degree-zero direct image is locally free and its natural fiber map is an isomorphism [ §7, Sätze 5 and 6 , Grauert1960 ] . The author's correction [ Grauert1963 ] concerns, in particular, a different bad-locus assertion in Satz 2; that assertion is not used here. A line bundle on a holomorphic submersion is flat over the base, since a submersion is locally a coordinate projection. The vanishing just proved and Euler-characteristic constancy therefore make $h^0(M_ y,A_ y^{\otimes k})$ constant. Consequently \[  E_ k=p_*A^{\otimes k},\qquad (E_ k)_ y\otimes \mathbb C(y)\simeq H^0(M_ y,A_ y^{\otimes k})  \] are respectively a locally free sheaf and its base-change isomorphism. Local freeness alone would not justify the latter. By the existing Kodaira embedding theorem , choose $k\geq k_0$ for which $A_{y_0}^{\otimes k}$ is very ample. Trivialize $E_ k$ after shrinking the base. The relative evaluation map is surjective on the central fiber. Its coherent cokernel has closed support missing that fiber; properness lets us shrink the base so that this support disappears. Evaluation then defines $G=(\Phi ,p):M_ U\to \mathbb P(E_ k^*)\simeq \mathbb P^ N\times U$, whose central fiber is the Kodaira embedding. The vertical differential of $\Phi $ is injective on the central fiber. Its rank-failure locus is closed; properness again permits a shrinking which removes it. The differential of $G$ is then injective, because its second component is $p$. If $G$ failed to be injective arbitrarily near $y_0$, there would be distinct $x_ j,x'_ j$ over $y_ j\to y_0$ with $G(x_ j)=G(x'_ j)$. Properness gives convergent subsequences, and the central-fiber embedding forces the two limits to coincide. Both sequences eventually lie in a single neighborhood on which the immersion $G$ is an embedding, a contradiction. After shrinking, $G$ is injective. It is proper as a map over $U$, hence is a closed holomorphic embedding. Evaluation identifies $G^*\mathcal O(1)$ with $A^{\otimes k}$. For disconnected fibers, the full space of sections is the direct sum over their finitely many components, and the complete linear system separates the components. For zero-dimensional fibers the same evaluation argument applies directly to finite reduced sets. $\square$

title: 9.72 Projective Hartogs extension
text: Ambient manifolds are connected unless stated otherwise. Fibers need not be connected; the section-envelope arguments treat their connected components separately. Lemma 9.72.1 . 0A2146B324EB Let $A$ be a closed analytic subset of complex codimension at least two in a complex manifold $U$. A meromorphic map $U\setminus A\dasharrow \mathbb P^ N$ extends meromorphically to $U$. Consequently, if $\mathcal E$ is a reflexive coherent sheaf on $U$, every saturated coherent subsheaf of $\mathcal E|_{U\setminus A}$ extends uniquely as a saturated coherent subsheaf of $\mathcal E$ on $U$. Proof. Use the existing normal meromorphic codimension-two extension theorem . For a map to $\mathbb P^ N$, choose a homogeneous coordinate not identically zero. All its affine coordinate ratios are meromorphic functions and extend by this argument. Clearing their finitely many local denominators defines the desired meromorphic projective map. The equations of any closed projective target, such as a Grassmannian, persist by density. For the sheaf assertion work locally and embed the reflexive ambient sheaf into a finite free sheaf, using generators of its dual and its canonical injection into its double dual. The subspace at the generic point gives a Grassmannian map; its Plücker ratios extend by the first part. Write the resulting meromorphic subspace as the kernel of a finite meromorphic matrix and clear denominators. Its intersection with the ambient coherent sheaf is the kernel of a holomorphic matrix on that sheaf, hence coherent. Its quotient embeds in a meromorphic vector space and is torsion-free, so it is saturated. On $U\setminus A$ it agrees with the original saturated sheaf. Saturated subsheaves are determined by their generic meromorphic subspaces, proving uniqueness and gluing. $\square$

title: 10.103 Euler characteristics under flat twists
text: Ambient manifolds are connected unless stated otherwise. Fibers need not be connected; the section-envelope arguments treat their connected components separately. Lemma 10.103.1 . E897B72A71BA If $\mathcal H$ is coherent on a smooth projective manifold and $\rho \in \operatorname {Pic}^0(Z)$, then $\chi (\mathcal H\otimes \rho )=\chi (\mathcal H)$. Proof. A coherent sheaf on smooth projective $Z$ has a finite resolution by vector bundles: repeatedly use ample global generation for a surjection and use regular local rings of dimension at most $\dim Z$ to terminate the kernels. Euler characteristic is additive in this resolution. For a vector bundle, the Dolbeault complex is elliptic and its index is locally constant under the continuous family of flat twists in the connected torus $\operatorname {Pic}^0(Z)$. A finite-dimensional kernel/cokernel reduction of a Fredholm operator shows this local constancy: after splitting off finite-dimensional complements, its remaining block is invertible for all nearby parameters. Its index is therefore constant along a path to the trivial twist. Summing over the resolution proves the formula. $\square$
